doc.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996

title: Teaching kids in Washington-area schools and Head Start
summary: Future plans and his 27 years of school concerts with a trio, drawing participation from children from Head Start to workshops for senior high.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: What’s coming up in the future for you? You’ve got the cruise.

Well just doing a lot of private festivals, kind of like this and so forth. And in the Washington area I’ve been for the last 27 years doing schools, with a trio. It started — this lady, Evelyn Audvin just started me off one day, “I hear you have some kids in school, you just moved to Maryland, and so if you’ve got as many kids as they say you have, you must be nice to kids.” Well that’s got nothing to do with being nice, I mean I know how to get ‘em. But she asked me to take the bass and go to a school up county in Montgomery County and I went up there. She picked me up and I went up, and she said, “you know if you could put some kind of program together, I could see you work up something for you to perform for the kids. So I got a piano player and a drummer and we started doing it. And through trial and error, because I always figured in order to deal with kids you have to be, you actually have to be a part of them. And so instead of talking IN to a kid and pushing down on him, PULL from him, and say what is this? You know this is called a bass fiddle. How do you think I would play this? And so I’m pulling.

Right. I say this is a bass fiddle and ba, ba, ba, ba, and that’s that. They get that with grown ups, with the parents, they get that with the teachers. “Which finger should I play this with?” And so it escalated and I’m doing about a hundred schools in the Washington area, that’s with Washington but I also do a Head Start, and I’ve been out there since ‘81. I do about 36 a year. And this is Wolf Trap I’m talking about.
Right. And you deal with pretty young kids too.

Three to five. Head Start. And then in Washington Performing Arts and doing the elementary schools in PG County, and sometimes PG County schools start at 8:00 and at 8:30 in the morning you’ve got to be 30 miles away. But when you walk in and you see these little eyes there, and you’re giving them something up close. And then the main thing is participation. Not just plain pushing, get them involved, and then they have an idea of what music is about aside from what they hear, and what’s force fed to them by the radios.
And it’s hopefully setting some seeds in their heads for the future.

We’ve had some very good results, some talented kids, and I’m speaking of like grade, and junior high. Senior high I just try to do mainly workshops because by the time they get up there they’re opinionated for what they want so when they have bands and choruses and so forth we do workshops for senior high and sometimes middle schools.
That’s a tough age sometimes, especially in large groups. The little kids are—
I go to some schools sometimes they’ve got twelve thousand. You know and middle school, gee whiz.
